newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MAIZE--S.Africa prices free for 1st time in 70 yrs.
newsitem.headline: MAIZE--S.Africa prices free for 1st time in 70 yrs.

text.p: For the first time in nearly 70 years South Africa's maize market will from next year be free of price control, a move observers say will hasten the demise of the state-owned Maize Board.

In a landmark decision on Thursday, Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom said a statutory floor price and stabilisation levy, in place since the early 1930s to support farmers, will be scrapped from the start of the new season in May.
"This means the end of the Maize Board at the start of the next season," said Piet Louw, manager of Unie Graan, a grain cooperative.
With the abolition of support prices, the board's main role, except its function as a player in the export market, falls away.
"It's export role will also come to an end," Louw said.
The board could not be reached for comment.

In October the board's general manager Leon du Plessis told Reuters it would be dissolved at the start of the 1997/98 season if the industry was able to agree on a blueprint for a future marketing system by then.

The minister's decision breaks an industry deadlock hit at a meeting last week when maize producers and co-ops called for a 490 rand a tonne floor price and processors, traders and other buyers strongly opposed such an intervention.
The decision received a mixed reception in the market.

The National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) slammed the move, saying a price "safety net" was needed as the market was not sophisticated enough to use other hedging mechanisms, including futures and forward contracting.
"The industry and minister have taken a very short-sighted decision," Japie Grobler, Nampo's chairman said.
He said farmers would plant less maize to prevent a surplus and lower prices. "It will turn South Africa into a net importer of maize," he told Reuters on Friday.
The South African Futures Exchange (Safex), which earlier this year began trading maize contracts, welcomed Hanekom's move.

"Safex believes that this move will not not only place maize farming in South Africa on a firmer economic basis...but it is also in line with worldwide trends and will be welcomed internationally," Safex said in a statement.
A maize futures trader said volumes in the futures market, which have been moderate until now, should be boosted in the next few months.
"This decision is a major happening in the market...The only way now to buy price protection is to use the futures market," the trader said.

Announcing the end of support on Thursday, Hanekom said farmers who were concerned about possible low prices for the next harvest should either arrange forward contracts and/or hedge their price risk on Safex.
The South African Poultry Association, which has recently suffered from high maize input costs, also praised the decision.

"(An already high local maize price due to strong global prices) was aggravated by abuse of the floor price system, which, in our view, was manipulated to create a shortage on the South African market for yellow maize," the association said in a statement.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
